cards.front: A severely unwell child with pneumonia is managed as [___]: oxygen, a fluid bolus, and prompt IV antibiotics — before any imaging.
cards.context:
The trio is a resuscitation bundle ordered by what kills fastest: hypoxia first, then circulatory failure, then the untreated infection.

Imaging never gates treatment — a drowsy, mottled or hypoxic child has all three running before any chest X-ray is taken.

cards.front: No chest rise while bagging a child: reposition the head, check the mask seal, open the mouth, [___], insert an adjunct, then go two-person.
cards.context:
The ladder runs cheapest-first because most failures are position or seal: re-tilt the head (neutral in infants, sniffing in children) and re-seat the mask before anything else.

Only then look inside: open the mouth, suction what you can actually see, and add a Guedel or nasopharyngeal airway if the tongue is the obstruction.

The endpoint is two-person bagging — one rescuer seals with both hands while the other squeezes. Still no rise: think foreign body or move to an advanced airway.

cards.front: Transient tachypnoea of the newborn is delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid; more common after caesarean delivery; resolves within [___] hours.
cards.context:
TTN is the commonest cause of respiratory distress in term/near-term infants in the first hours of life — delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid.

Clinical: tachypnoea 60-100/min, mild work of breathing, minimal O₂ need (FiO₂ <0.4). CXR shows 'wet lungs' — fluid in the horizontal fissure, perihilar streaking, hyperinflation.

Caesarean raises risk (no chest squeeze/catecholamine surge to absorb fluid). Self-limiting diagnosis of exclusion; trap is mistaking it for sepsis or RDS, so septic screen ± antibiotics until ruled out.

cards.front: In most infants with slow weight gain, the main problem is inadequate [___] intake.
cards.context: Review feeding volume and technique before ordering broad tests. Nutrition drives growth particularly strongly below age two.

cards.front: Jaundice in the first [___] hours of life is ALWAYS pathological — usually haemolysis (ABO/Rh, G6PD), sepsis, or congenital infection (TORCH: Toxoplasma, Other, Rubella, CMV, Herpes); check direct Coombs.
cards.context: First-24-hour jaundice is always pathological — physiological jaundice peaks day 3-5. Day 1 jaundice usually means haemolysis (ABO/Rh incompatibility, G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis), sepsis.

cards.front: Innocent murmurs are heard in up to [___]% of healthy children; require no treatment; remember the 7 S's (soft, systolic, asymptomatic, short, sitting diminishes, single, sensitive).
cards.context:
Innocent (functional) murmurs are heard in up to 30% of healthy children — extremely common, reflecting normal turbulent flow rather than structural disease.

Reassure and observe.

Refer for echo if any pathological features (diastolic, harsh, pansystolic, abnormal S2, symptomatic).

cards.front: Because a child's compliant ribs transmit force without fracturing, the most common traumatic chest injury in children is pulmonary [___].
cards.context:
Elastic paediatric ribs bow rather than break, so energy passes straight to the lung parenchyma. Significant intrathoracic injury can exist with no rib fracture and a deceptively normal early chest X-ray.

Rib fractures in a young child therefore signal massive force — or non-accidental injury.

cards.front: HUS triad: microangiopathic haemolytic [___] (schistocytes, raised LDH, low haptoglobin), thrombocytopenia (consumed in microthrombi), and acute kidney injury. Typical (D+) HUS follows bloody diarrhoea from Shiga-toxin-producing *E. coli*.
cards.context:
HUS (haemolytic uraemic syndrome) triad: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (schistocytes on film, raised LDH, low haptoglobin), thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury (rising creatinine, oliguria).

Typical (D+ HUS) follows bloody diarrhoea from Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (O157:H7); 5-10 days latency.

Treatment is supportive — antibiotics may worsen disease.

cards.front: Use WHO growth charts for 0-2 years and [___] charts for 2-18 years; serial trends matter more than a single measurement.
cards.context:
WHO 0–2 charts use breastfed-infant data as the reference standard. From 2–18 years RCH uses CDC charts — they are US-developed, and they are still the Australian recommendation, not a US-only rule.

What matters is the trend, not a single value. Crossing 2 percentile lines downward triggers a failure-to-thrive workup.

cards.front: The child-protection aphorism is that those who do not [___] rarely bruise.
cards.context:
The aphorism is doing real work: bruises come from a child colliding with the world, so a child who cannot move should not have them.

Accidental bruises cluster over bony prominences on the front of a mobile child, especially the shins and forehead.

Bruising on the ears, neck, torso or buttocks, or any bruise before independent movement, needs explaining.

cards.front: Two serious complications of osteomyelitis are spread to the adjacent joint causing [___], and growth-plate damage causing limb-length discrepancy.
cards.context: Untreated or chronic osteomyelitis spreads to the neighbouring joint and damages the adjacent growth plate, so a delayed presentation risks both an infected joint and a future limb-length problem.

cards.front: In paediatric heart failure, peripheral oedema is [___] common than in adults, while hepatomegaly is a particularly useful sign of systemic venous congestion.
cards.context:
Paediatric heart failure often presents with tachypnoea, poor feeding, sweating and faltering growth. Systemic venous congestion commonly produces hepatomegaly, making the liver a particularly useful examination target.

Peripheral oedema is less common than in adult heart failure, but it can occur, especially with advanced or right-sided congestion — it is not absent in children.

cards.front: Legal authority to make medical decisions for a child rests with whoever holds [___] responsibility, not simply whichever adult accompanies the child.
cards.context:
Parental responsibility is the legal authority to make decisions for a child — it is not the same as being the person who brought them in.

A grandparent, older sibling or family friend at the bedside usually cannot consent. Ask who holds parental responsibility before you ask them to sign anything.

Court orders can move it, and both parents retain it after separation unless an order says otherwise.

cards.front: Suspect empyema in paediatric pneumonia if fever persists beyond 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics; bedside [___] is most sensitive for loculation.
cards.context:
Persistent fever beyond 48 h of appropriate antibiotics in paediatric pneumonia is the standard empyema trigger — bacteria seed the pleural space adjacent to inflamed lung, organising into a loculated collection.

Workup: CXR, bedside USS (most sensitive for loculation), CT if complex.

cards.front: Avulsed primary (baby) teeth should NOT be replanted — risks damage to the developing successor tooth bud. Avulsed permanent teeth should be replanted within 60 minutes; if delayed, store in [___] (or saline / buccal sulcus) to preserve the periodontal ligament.
cards.context:
Replantation rule splits by tooth type. PERMANENT: replant within 60 min (ideally <15 min); handle by crown only, rinse gently (preserves periodontal ligament), store in milk or saline if can't replant immediately.

PRIMARY (baby): do NOT replant — risks damaging the developing permanent tooth bud (ankylosis, infection, developmental disturbance).

Practical: adult/older child permanent tooth → milk, dentist within 30-60 min; toddler baby tooth → don't replant, dentist to assess remaining teeth and soft tissue (permanent teeth erupt age 6+).

cards.front: A patient with cyanotic congenital heart disease has deoxygenated blood that bypasses the lungs and reaches the systemic circulation un-oxygenated. The shunt is [___].
cards.context:
In cyanotic congenital heart disease, deoxygenated blood crosses a right-to-left shunt and bypasses the lungs.

Classic lesions include tetralogy of Fallot, transposition, truncus arteriosus, tricuspid atresia, and total anomalous pulmonary venous return.

cards.front: Alkaline phosphatase in a healthy, growing school-age child normally reaches about 350 U/L, because roughly half the circulating enzyme comes from [___] laying down new bone.
cards.context:
Alkaline phosphatase is the classic paediatric trap, because roughly half the circulating enzyme in a child comes from bone rather than the biliary tree.

A growing child therefore runs three to four times the adult upper limit as a matter of course, and the value peaks again during the pubertal growth spurt before falling to adult levels once the growth plates fuse.

Reading a child's ALP against an adult range generates a liver referral for normal growth.

cards.front: A teenager with sore throat, fever, marked cervical lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly likely has infectious [___].
cards.context: Recognise the picture: an adolescent with a prolonged sore throat, fever, prominent posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and fatigue, often with splenomegaly (advise no contact sport — splenic rupture risk).

cards.front: Croup is a [___] diagnosis; alarm features include agitation, drowsiness, persistent stridor at rest. hypoxia is a late sign — by then the child is in respiratory failure.
cards.context:
Croup is a clinical diagnosis — barking cough plus inspiratory stridor in a 1-2 year old. Imaging doesn't change management; reserve for atypical cases or to rule out foreign body.

Hypoxia is a LATE sign because croup obstruction is mainly inspiratory; by the time SpO2 drops, the child is in significant respiratory failure.

cards.front: In paediatric heart failure, peripheral oedema is less common than in adults, while [___] is a particularly useful sign of systemic venous congestion.
cards.context:
Paediatric heart failure often presents with tachypnoea, poor feeding, sweating and faltering growth. Systemic venous congestion commonly produces hepatomegaly, making the liver a particularly useful examination target.

Peripheral oedema is less common than in adult heart failure, but it can occur, especially with advanced or right-sided congestion — it is not absent in children.

cards.front: Unlike the sparse posterior-pole bleeds of accidental injury, the retinal haemorrhages of abusive head trauma are multi-layered, too numerous to count, and characteristically extend to the peripheral [___].
cards.context:
The discriminating feature that separates abuse from accident: haemorrhages spanning all retinal layers and reaching the far peripheral retina (the ora serrata) reflect the vitreoretinal traction of repetitive shaking.

A dilated fundoscopic exam by ophthalmology is mandatory — few, unilateral posterior haemorrhages are non-specific.

cards.front: Consolidation obliterating the left heart border lies in the [___], part of the left upper lobe.
cards.context:
The left-sided counterpart of the right middle lobe, and the reason the left heart border can vanish.

The lingula is part of the left upper lobe and lies against the left heart border. Consolidation there obliterates that border.

cards.front: Gillick competence lets a child consent to treatment, but a competent child's [___] of life-sustaining treatment may still be overridden by a court.
cards.context:
A competent child's CONSENT is effective. Their REFUSAL of life-sustaining treatment can still be overridden by a court or, in some circumstances, by a person with parental responsibility.

The asymmetry is deliberate and often surprises students: the law is more willing to let a child say yes to treatment than to let them say no to survival.

cards.front: Under the RCH neonatal pathway, empiric antibiotics may be ceased at [___] hours when cultures remain negative and the infant is well.
cards.context:
Empiric treatment is a time-limited safety intervention, not an automatic full course.

Under RCH, EOS or LOS antibiotics can cease at 36 hours when cultures show no growth and the infant is clinically well; an identified alternative diagnosis may support earlier cessation in LOS.

Persistent illness, a positive culture or abnormal CSF changes the plan.

cards.front: A 6-year-old boy has a painless limp and a positive Trendelenburg. He is not overweight. This age band is [___], not slipped capital femoral epiphysis.
cards.context: Perthes is 4–10; SCFE is the overweight 10–14-year-old. A 6-year-old with Trendelenburg is the younger band — general 'boy with a limp' is not enough.

cards.front: Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) F:M ratio is 6:1 — the only hip condition with female preponderance; incidence ~[___] in 1000 live births.
cards.context:
DDH is a spectrum from subluxable through dislocatable to fully dislocated. Incidence ~4 in 1000 live births, F:M ratio 6:1 — the only hip condition with strong female predominance (maternal hormone ligamentous laxity).

Risk factors (5 Fs): Female, Firstborn, Family history, Feet down (breech), Fluid low (oligohydramnios). Routine screening at birth + 6-week check.

cards.front: When neonatal meningitis is suspected, replace the gentamicin-only Gram-negative strategy with benzylpenicillin plus a third-generation [___] that penetrates CSF.
cards.context:
Neonatal meningitis must cover GBS, E. coli and Listeria and reach therapeutic CSF concentrations. Gentamicin is useful for bloodstream Gram-negative synergy but penetrates CSF unreliably.

RCH therefore pairs benzylpenicillin with a third-generation cephalosporin; cefotaxime is generally preferred to ceftriaxone in neonates.

cards.front: In an injured child, hypotension appears only after roughly [___]% of circulating volume is lost — rely on tachycardia, cool peripheries and capillary refill to detect shock earlier.
cards.context:
Children vasoconstrict and mount tachycardia so effectively that blood pressure holds until a large fraction of the circulating volume is gone — a normal reading never excludes serious haemorrhage.

By the time pressure falls the child is peri-arrest, which is why hypotension in a child is treated as a pre-terminal sign.

cards.front: A neonate with bilious vomiting on day 1 has a 'double-bubble' on AXR. Approximately [___]% of these cases are associated with Down syndrome.
cards.context:
On abdominal X-ray, duodenal atresia shows the 'double-bubble' sign — air in the stomach and proximal duodenum, no distal gas, separated by the pylorus.

Always check for a chromosomal association: ~30% of duodenal atresia cases have trisomy 21. The AXR finding should prompt karyotype review and a search for other anomalies (cardiac, anorectal).

cards.front: A flat, well-demarcated vascular birthmark that persists and does NOT fade or involute is a [___].
cards.context: A port-wine stain is a capillary malformation — unlike an infantile haemangioma it does not proliferate or involute. A V1 trigeminal distribution warrants screening for Sturge-Weber syndrome.

cards.front: After treated scarlet fever, a child develops cola urine and oedema. The GP explains that penicillin reduces the risk of [___], rather than reliably preventing this renal complication.
cards.context:
Treating group A streptococcal pharyngitis reduces acute rheumatic fever risk. Evidence is insufficient to establish that antibiotics prevent post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

The later nephritic illness can therefore occur despite appropriate antibiotics. It still needs assessment of blood pressure, renal function and fluid balance.

cards.front: The first-line corticosteroid for a child with croup and stridor is oral [___].
cards.context:
Croup is laryngotracheal oedema from a parainfluenza virus, and oedema is what narrows the subglottis and produces the barking cough and stridor.

Oral dosing is preferred over IV or nebulised when a child with stridor can take medicine, and the half-life is long enough to cover the typical natural history.

cards.front: Low birthweight is associated with a reduced [___] number, which may increase susceptibility to later kidney disease.
cards.context:
Low birthweight is associated with fewer nephrons and greater later kidney-disease risk. This is a risk relationship, not an inevitable outcome for an individual child.

Past post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is also associated with later albuminuria. Recurrent skin or throat infection should not be presented as proof of a congenital nephron deficit.

cards.front: Holliday-Segar maintenance: first 10 kg = [___] mL/kg/day; second 10 kg = 50 mL/kg/day; each kg after = 20 mL/kg/day.
cards.context:
Daily Holliday-Segar maintenance uses 100/50/20 mL/kg/day for successive weight bands. For 25 kg, this gives 1600 mL/day, or about 67 mL/hour when divided by 24.

The hourly 4-2-1 rule gives 65 mL/hour for the same child. Both are accepted starting estimates, not exact unit conversions.

Adjust for illness and fluid balance; unwell children often need less than full maintenance. Isotonic fluid with glucose is usually preferred.

cards.front: A febrile infant aged 28 days or younger by corrected age needs blood, urine and CSF investigation plus admission for empiric [___] antibiotics.
cards.context:
RCH uses corrected age. An infant aged 28 days or younger with fever needs FBE, CRP, blood culture, an uncontaminated urine specimen, CSF studies and chest imaging when respiratory infection is suspected.

The infant is admitted for empiric IV therapy even if feeding and examination initially look normal.

cards.front: Malabsorption diarrhoea types: fatty (steatorrhoea, fat malabsorption); watery (osmotic or secretory); [___] (infection, IBD).
cards.context:
The character of diarrhoea narrows the cause. Fatty (steatorrhoea — pale, greasy, foul, floats) → fat malabsorption (CF, pancreatic insufficiency, biliary disease, coeliac).

Watery → osmotic (lactose intolerance) or secretory (toxin, hormone, bile salt). Bloody → infection, IBD, milk protein intolerance.

cards.front: Under the Australian Asthma Handbook lung-function criterion for ages 6–11, a positive bronchodilator response is an absolute FEV1 increase of at least [___]% of predicted FEV1 after salbutamol.
cards.context:
Reversibility is the physiological signature spirometry is asked to demonstrate: obstruction that improves convincingly after a bronchodilator supports asthma over fixed narrowing.

The Australian Asthma Handbook lung-function (ERS/ATS) criterion uses an absolute rise of at least 10% of predicted FEV1. The NAC Spirometry Handbook uses at least 12% of the pre-bronchodilator reading.

Both conventions appear in the Australian handbook: the denominator matters, and neither requires the adult 200 mL minimum.

cards.front: A full antibiotic course for scarlet fever reduces acute [___] fever, but does not reliably prevent post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
cards.context:
Treating Group A streptococcal pharyngitis or scarlet fever eradicates the organism and reduces the risk of acute rheumatic fever.

The same course does not reliably prevent post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which is an immune-complex complication.

cards.front: The bedside manoeuvre that shows a rib hump in a structural spinal curve while a postural curve disappears completely is [___].
cards.context:
Rotation is what makes a curve structural: the vertebrae twist and carry the ribs with them, so the hump rises on the convex side.

A postural curve has no rotation, vanishes lying down and never becomes structural. Sitting the child down removes any contribution from unequal leg length.

cards.front: ITP: most common paediatric thrombocytopenia, usually [___] weeks post-viral, self-limiting in 80% within 6 months; if other cell lines abnormal — suspect malignancy.
cards.context:
Immune thrombocytopaenic purpura (ITP) is the commonest cause of thrombocytopenia in well children. Typical presentation 1-4 weeks after viral infection — autoantibody-mediated platelet destruction.

Petechiae, bruising, mucosal bleeding; everything else (FBC otherwise normal, no organomegaly, no constitutional symptoms) normal. Self-limiting in 80% within 6 months.

If anything else abnormal — suspect malignancy.

cards.front: Universal newborn hearing screen target ages: screen by 1 month, diagnose by [___] months, intervene by 6 months — closes the critical window for language development.
cards.context:
The 1-3-6 rule for newborn hearing screening: screen by 1 month (OAE first-line, ABR for NICU), confirm any failed screen with audiology by 3 months. Start intervention (hearing aids, early-intervention) by 6 months.

The targets aren't arbitrary — the first 6 months are the critical language-scaffolding window, and delays past it measurably impair lifelong speech outcomes.

In Australia ~98% are screened by 1 month; compliance falls off at diagnosis and intervention, which is where infants slip through.

cards.front: In cystic fibrosis, the defective cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) channel produces thick, dehydrated airway secretions; impaired mucociliary clearance drives chronic infection and progressive [___].
cards.context:
CFTR normally exports chloride into airway lumen, drawing water with it to keep mucus hydrated for cilial clearance.

Once bronchiectasis develops, the cycle is self-sustaining.

cards.front: A flat 5-year-old is in asystole with no IV access, so the team drills the tibia. The correctly formatted request is 'Adrenaline, [___] mL of 1-in-10,000, IO, stat' — a dose of 180 micrograms.
cards.context:
The silent chain: (5 + 4) x 2 = 18 kg; 18 x 10 microg/kg = 180 microg; at 100 microg/mL that is 1.8 mL.

Nothing about the drug changes by route — IO doses are identical to IV, so the request format only swaps the route word.

In arrest with no access in place, the drill comes out first: straight to IO, adrenaline immediately, then every second loop.

cards.front: Bacterial conjunctivitis stays on the surface of the eye, so a child whose eye is glued shut with pus each morning is usually systemically well, with no [___].
cards.context:
The infection is local, so the child is systemically well and treatment is topical. Most cases settle within 7 days; chloramphenicol drops speed recovery modestly.

A raised temperature changes the question. In a young child look at the ears for conjunctivitis-otitis syndrome from Haemophilus influenzae, and at the lids for periorbital cellulitis.

A sticky eye in a neonate is different again: gonococcal and chlamydial infection need swabs and systemic antibiotics, not drops alone.

cards.front: After adrenaline in anaphylaxis with hypotension, give a normal saline bolus of [___] mL/kg.
cards.context: Anaphylactic shock is distributive: adrenaline restores vascular tone, but a vasodilated, fluid-leaky circulation also needs volume. Give the crystalloid bolus after adrenaline, not instead of it.

cards.front: Treat pertussis with azithromycin; vaccinated individuals may have milder disease but remain [___].
cards.context:
Azithromycin (5-day course) eradicates Bordetella from the respiratory tract and limits transmission; once the paroxysmal cough is toxin-driven it does little for the patient.

Vaccine protection is incomplete and wanes, so vaccinated people can still develop (usually milder, atypical) pertussis and transmit it — the 'vaccinated but contagious' phenomenon.

This is why adolescents and adults receive boosters, and why maternal pertussis vaccination is given in pregnancy to protect newborns.

cards.front: A well 3-year-old has a bulging tympanic membrane, an effusion and no discharge. The appropriate first step is analgesia plus watchful waiting for 48 hours; the single feature in the history that would most clearly override this in an infant is age under [___] months.
cards.context:
Most uncomplicated acute otitis media is analgesia and 48 hours of watchful waiting. The examinable skill is who should NOT wait.

Age under 6 months, systemic illness, discharge, craniofacial anomaly, immunocompromise, a cochlear implant, and high-risk Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children all lower the threshold.

Bilateral disease under 2 is not by itself an automatic RCH indication — follow the local antimicrobial guideline.

cards.front: Bilateral leg pain in the evening or at night with a normal exam and no daytime symptoms is [___] pains.
cards.context: A benign diagnosis of exclusion. The reassuring pattern: bilateral, evening/night, normal exam, and completely well by morning with no limp or daytime symptoms. Unilateral or daytime pain should make you look harder.

cards.front: Distinguishing congenital diaphragmatic hernia from cystic adenomatoid malformation on a plain film turns on whether the chest lucencies are continuous with the abdominal gas pattern; in the hernia the abdomen additionally looks [___].
cards.context:
Both produce cystic lucencies in a hemithorax, and the discriminator is anatomical continuity rather than the cysts themselves.

In a diaphragmatic hernia the lucencies ARE bowel, so they run continuously into the abdominal gas pattern, and the abdomen looks gasless.

 A cystic adenomatoid malformation is lung tissue: the cysts stop at the diaphragm and the abdominal gas pattern is normal. Passing a nasogastric tube settles it when its tip appears in the chest.

cards.front: Wet combing of an itchy schoolchild’s scalp recovers a live crawling insect. The infestation is [___].
cards.context:
Finding live lice confirms active infestation; attached eggs alone can persist after treatment. Itching reflects a reaction to bites and may be delayed after acquisition.

Examine close contacts and use a treatment method that addresses the life cycle.

cards.front: A bright red, lobulated vascular lesion that appears in the first weeks, grows, then involutes over years is an infantile [___].
cards.context: The natural history is the key: NOT usually present at birth, appears in the first weeks, proliferates for months, then slowly involutes over years. Most need nothing but reassurance.

cards.front: Autism spectrum disorder prevalence is ~1-2%, skewed toward males with an M:F ratio of approximately [___]; typically detected before school entry.
cards.context:
Autism spectrum disorder prevalence is around 1-2%, with M:F ratio approximately 4:1 (though females may be under-diagnosed due to better masking).

Intellectual disability is a possible but not necessary comorbidity (about a third of ASD have ID).

Earlier diagnosis enables earlier intervention with measurable outcome benefit.

cards.front: A nasopharyngeal airway is sized from the nostril to the tragus of the ear, and is avoided in a suspected [___] fracture.
cards.context:
The nasopharyngeal airway is the adjunct for the child WITH a gag reflex — semi-conscious, obstructing, but not flat. Size it from the nostril to the tragus of the ear.

The classic contraindication is suspected base-of-skull fracture — the tube can follow the fracture line intracranially. Adenoidal bleeding is the common minor complication in children.

cards.front: A child with epiglottitis drools because the swollen supraglottis makes [___] too painful.
cards.context:
Drooling is an obstruction sign, not a salivation problem: the swollen supraglottis turns each attempt to clear saliva into pain and a threat to the airway, so secretions spill out instead.

The same anatomy explains the absent bark — the subglottis and cords are untouched, so there is no seal-like cough. Croup is the mirror image: barking cough, no drooling.

cards.front: Hepatitis A spreads by the [___] route (contaminated food/water, dirty hands), whereas Hepatitis B spreads via infected blood and vertical (mother-to-baby) transmission.
cards.context:
The two paediatric hepatitis viruses spread completely differently, and that drives prevention.

Hep A passes person-to-person via contaminated food/water and dirty hands (childcare, travel, outbreaks) so hygiene + vaccine prevent it.

Hep B passes via infected body fluids; in children the dominant route worldwide is vertical at birth, which is why the Hep B vaccine is given as a birth dose.

cards.front: A 6-year-old fell from monkey bars onto an outstretched hand. The lateral elbow film shows a supracondylar fracture angulated backwards, with the posterior cortex still in continuity. This is Gartland [___].
cards.context:
Gartland grades extension supracondylar fractures on the lateral film by what has happened to the posterior cortex.

Undisplaced is type I. Angulated with the posterior cortex intact is type II. Complete displacement with no cortical contact is type III.

The cortex matters because type III carries the highest neurovascular risk and needs urgent orthopaedic reduction and pinning.

cards.front: Alkaline phosphatase in a healthy, growing school-age child normally reaches about [___] U/L, because roughly half the circulating enzyme comes from osteoblasts laying down new bone.
cards.context:
Alkaline phosphatase is the classic paediatric trap, because roughly half the circulating enzyme in a child comes from bone rather than the biliary tree.

A growing child therefore runs three to four times the adult upper limit as a matter of course, and the value peaks again during the pubertal growth spurt before falling to adult levels once the growth plates fuse.

Reading a child's ALP against an adult range generates a liver referral for normal growth.

cards.front: Burns Rule of 9s: modified in children because head is a larger proportion (use Lund-Browder); fluid resuscitation if ≥[___]% TBSA (paediatric burn-fluid formula).
cards.context:
Burns assessment uses Rule of 9s, but children differ — head is a larger BSA proportion. Adult head = 9% TBSA; infant head = 18%, decreasing with age. Use the Lund-Browder chart for accuracy under 10 years.

 Fluid resuscitation is triggered at ≥10% TBSA partial-/full-thickness burns.

Current specialist paediatric guidance uses 3 mL Hartmann's × kg × %TBSA over 24 hours, plus separate maintenance fluid; give half the calculated burn-resuscitation volume in the first 8 hours from the time of injury.

cards.front: Nephritic syndrome features: haematuria (often cola-coloured), [___], and mild-moderate proteinuria; commonest paediatric cause is PSGN.
cards.context:
Nephritic syndrome reflects glomerular INFLAMMATION (contrast nephrotic = podocyte leak).

Inflamed glomeruli let red cells through, so haematuria with RBC casts is the hallmark, and proteinuria stays mild-to-moderate rather than nephrotic-range.

Falling GFR causes salt and water retention, which drives the hypertension and oedema. Cola/tea-coloured urine reflects RBC breakdown in acidic urine.

cards.front: First-line serological investigation for suspected coeliac disease is [___] IgA.
cards.context:
Tissue transglutaminase is the autoantigen in coeliac disease — anti-TTG IgA is the most direct, specific, sensitive serological screen, and cheap.

Most important test-discipline point: do NOT start a gluten-free diet before testing — withdrawal normalises serology + makes biopsy non-diagnostic, leading to lifelong unconfirmed diagnosis.

cards.front: Paediatric bones: thicker [___] (faster healing), physis is weak point (fractures more common than dislocations), more porous (bend before break).
cards.context:
Three differences from adult bone: (1) thick periosteum acts as an internal splint — faster healing, less displacement.

(2) the open physis (growth plate) is the weakest link, so it fails before the joint, making fractures commoner than dislocations; (3) more porous bone bends or buckles before it snaps (greenstick, torus).

cards.front: Live vaccines (MMR, varicella, rotavirus, BCG, LAIV, yellow fever) are contraindicated in immunocompromise and [___]; minor illness is NOT a contraindication.
cards.context:
Live vaccines (MMR, varicella, rotavirus, BCG, LAIV, yellow fever, Zostavax) contain weakened but replicating organisms — strong immunity, but risk of vaccine-strain disease in immunocompromised hosts.

Absolute contraindications: pregnancy and severe immunocompromise (HIV with low CD4, active malignancy, high-dose immunosuppressants, post-SCT).

cards.front: Erythema toxicum neonatorum needs [___] treatment.
cards.context:
Erythema toxicum is the rash the newborn check finds most often: blotchy red macules 2-3 cm across, each with a tiny central papule, vesicle or pustule, over the chest, back, face and proximal limbs.

It spares the palms and soles. It is benign and self-limited and needs no treatment.

The value of knowing it well is that it lets you recognise the rashes that do NOT fit — grouped vesicles on a red base (herpes), or pustules present at birth.

cards.front: Scribbling, trying a spoon, drinking from an open cup, following a gesture-free one-step direction and copying a household chore fit the [___]-month profile.
cards.context:
The eighteen-month profile tests more than walking and vocabulary. It includes scribbling, trying a spoon, drinking from an open cup, following a gesture-free one-step direction and copying a simple household task.

This constellation samples fine motor, self-care, receptive language and cognition together.

cards.front: In TORCH, the letters stand for toxoplasmosis, other, rubella, cytomegalovirus and [___] simplex.
cards.context:
TORCH is a memory aid for the infections a mother can pass to her baby before or around birth: Toxoplasmosis, Other, Rubella, Cytomegalovirus and Herpes simplex.

The 'Other' bucket is doing a lot of work — it holds syphilis, varicella, parvovirus B19, HIV, listeria and more recently Zika.

Many clinicians now think the acronym is past its use-by date for exactly that reason, but it is still how the topic is taught and examined.

cards.front: Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) increases future suicide risk by 4-7×; never dismiss 'superficial' injuries — assess lethality, intent, and underlying [___] distress.
cards.context:
NSSI is usually emotion regulation or communication, not intent to die — but it overlaps with suicide. NSSI raises future suicide attempt risk 4-7×, so 'superficial cutting for attention' should never be dismissed.

Assess function, method/lethality (depth, location, dose), intent at the time, current intent, and access to means.
